questions.stem: Which of the following words contains exactly three phonemes?
options: fox
straight
thought
eight
questions.why: Phonemes are counted by sound, not by letter. 'Thought' has seven letters but only three phonemes: /θ/ (spelled th), one vowel (spelled ough), and /t/, so /θɔt/. Digraphs and complex vowel spellings often stand for a single phoneme, while a single letter such as x can stand for two (/ks/).

traps.note: Three letters, but x stands for two sounds, /k/ and /s/, so 'fox' has four phonemes: /f/ /ɑ/ /k/ /s/.
A blend like str is three phonemes, not one unit, and aigh spells one diphthong, so 'straight' has five: /s/ /t/ /r/ /eɪ/ /t/. Only digraphs such as sh or th spell a single sound.
The diphthong /eɪ/ counts as one vowel phoneme and gh is silent, so 'eight' has only two phonemes: /eɪ/ and /t/.

questions.key: Count phonemes by sound, not letters: thought = /θ/ + vowel + /t/ (3); the x in fox = /ks/ (2).

questions.stem: A teacher points out that the th in 'think' and the th in 'this' sound different. Which of the following best describes these two sounds?
options: They are two separate phonemes, /θ/ and /ð/, that differ only in voicing.
They are one phoneme, since both are spelled with the same digraph, th.
They are two allophones of /t/ that occur in different word positions.
They are two separate phonemes that differ in their place of articulation.
questions.why: /θ/ (think) and /ð/ (this) are both made by pushing air between the tongue and the upper teeth (interdental fricatives); the only difference is that /ð/ is voiced, with the vocal folds vibrating. They are separate phonemes because swapping them can change a word, as in the minimal pair 'teeth' /tiθ/ (noun) and 'teethe' /tið/ (verb). Spelling is not evidence: English uses one digraph for two phonemes.

traps.note: Spelling doesn't determine phonemes. The digraph th spells two different phonemes, and the minimal pair teeth/teethe proves they contrast.
Allophones are predictable variants of one phoneme that never change meaning. These sounds do change meaning, and neither is a variant of /t/.
Both sounds are made at the same place (tongue at the teeth) in the same manner (fricative); voicing is the only difference.

questions.key: /θ/ (think) and /ð/ (this) are separate phonemes that differ only in voicing: teeth vs. teethe.

questions.stem: In English, the /p/ in 'pin' is pronounced with a puff of air, [pʰ], while the /p/ in 'spin' has none, [p]. Native speakers hear them as the same sound. Which term best describes [pʰ] and [p] in English?
options: a minimal pair
allophones of one phoneme
two contrasting phonemes
two sounds in free variation
questions.why: Allophones are predictable variants of a single phoneme that never change a word's meaning. English voiceless stops are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable (pin [pʰɪn]) and unaspirated after /s/ (spin [spɪn]), so the two never contrast. In Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, and Korean, aspiration does distinguish words, which shows that a difference that is 'invisible' in one language can be meaningful in another.

traps.note: A minimal pair is two words that differ by one phoneme (pin/bin). [pʰ] and [p] are sounds, not words, and they never create different words in English.
Contrasting phonemes change meaning when swapped. Swapping [pʰ] and [p] in English only sounds odd; it never produces a different word.
In free variation either sound can occur in the same spot. Here the choice is predictable from position (aspirated initially, unaspirated after /s/).

questions.key: Allophones are predictable variants of one phoneme ([pʰ] in pin, [p] in spin); they never change meaning.

questions.stimulus:
Oral reading record, grade 4 Integrated ENL (Emerging; home language Spanish)
Text: “The students speak Spanish at school.”
Student: “The estudents espeak Espanish at eschool.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the pattern in this student's oral reading?
options: Spanish words cannot begin with /s/ followed by a consonant, so the student adds a vowel before the cluster.
Spanish lacks the /s/ phoneme, so the student substitutes the closest Spanish sound sequence for it.
The student may have a reading disability, since the added sounds do not appear in the printed words.
The student is simplifying each cluster by deleting a consonant, a common strategy in early speech.
questions.why: Every language has phonotactic rules about which sound sequences may occur. Spanish has /s/ and has clusters like /pl/ and /tr/, but no Spanish word begins with /s/ + consonant (compare estudiante, España, escuela). The student repairs the unfamiliar English cluster by inserting /e/ before it, a process called epenthesis. This is negative transfer of L1 syllable structure, not a reading problem.

traps.note: Spanish has the /s/ phoneme (sí, casa), and the student pronounces it. The problem is where /s/ may occur, a phonotactic constraint, not a missing sound.
The pattern is systematic and predicted by the home language's sound rules, which is typical L2 transfer. Calling it a disability confuses a language difference with a disorder.
Nothing is deleted; the student keeps every consonant and adds a vowel. Inserting a sound to repair a cluster is epenthesis.

questions.key: Spanish speakers' 'espeak/estudent' is epenthesis: L1 phonotactics forbid word-initial /s/ + consonant.

questions.stimulus: A grade 6 student (Transitioning; home language Spanish) tells the class, “I leave in Queens with my grandmother,” meaning live. In other lessons, he pronounces 'ship' and 'sheep' the same way.
questions.stem: Which minimal pair would be most useful for targeted practice of the contrast behind these errors?
options: fill / fell
leave / leaf
fill / feel
live / lives
questions.why: Both errors show the student merging /ɪ/ (live, ship) and /i/ (leave, sheep). Spanish has a five-vowel system with a single high front vowel, so this English contrast is new. A minimal pair is two words that differ in exactly one phoneme in the same position, and 'fill / feel' isolates exactly the /ɪ/–/i/ contrast the student needs.

traps.note: 'Fill / fell' is a true minimal pair, but it contrasts /ɪ/ with /ɛ/, not the /ɪ/–/i/ contrast this student is merging.
This pair borrows a word from the stimulus but contrasts final /v/ and /f/ (voicing). The student's problem is the vowel, not the final consonant.
'Live / lives' differ by an added morpheme, not by one substituted phoneme in the same position, so it isn't a minimal pair and doesn't target the vowel.

questions.key: Choose minimal pairs that isolate the exact merged contrast: /ɪ/–/i/ → fill/feel, ship/sheep, live/leave.

questions.stimulus:
Teacher says | Student writes
right | light
load | road
collect | correct
glass | grass
questions.stem: A grade 7 Transitioning student whose home language is Korean produced these spellings on a dictation task. The pattern is most likely the result of which of the following?
options: In Korean, [l] and a flap [ɾ] are variants of one phoneme, so the English /r/–/l/ contrast is hard to perceive.
Korean has neither an r-like nor an l-like sound, so the student is guessing between two completely unfamiliar sounds.
The student is reversing letters while writing, which is an early sign of a visual-processing disability.
English spelling is irregular, so the student cannot reliably predict which letter represents each sound.
questions.why: Korean has one liquid phoneme (ㄹ) that is pronounced as a flap [ɾ] in some positions and as [l] in others. Because the difference is predictable by position, Korean speakers learn to ignore it, so English minimal pairs like right/light and collect/correct can sound alike. When two sounds are allophones in the L1 but separate phonemes in English, learners struggle both to hear and to produce the contrast.

traps.note: Korean speakers do produce both [l] and an r-like flap. What Korean lacks is a meaningful contrast between them, so the student needs perception practice, not new sounds.
The substitutions go both ways and only between r and l, exactly where Korean merges the sounds. That's predictable L1 transfer, not evidence of a disability.
English spelling is irregular in many places, but r and l are spelled consistently. The errors follow sounds the student can't yet distinguish.

questions.key: Two L1 allophones become one category for the learner: Korean ㄹ covers [l] and [ɾ], so right/light merge.

questions.stimulus: During a grade 5 science discussion, a student (Emerging; home language Arabic) says, “We put the blant by the window,” and later asks, “Can I have a ben?”
questions.stem: The ENL teacher wants to address this pronunciation pattern. Which approach would be most effective?
options: Correct each mispronounced word immediately whenever the student speaks in discussions, so the model is heard often.
Assign a daily list of forty words beginning with p for the student to read aloud until the sound becomes automatic.
Practice pairs like pea/bee and pack/back, show the puff of air for /p/ with a paper strip, then use them in sentences.
Refer the student to the speech-language pathologist, since the substitution has continued for months despite modeling.
questions.why: Arabic has /b/ but no /p/ phoneme, so learners often substitute /b/ for English /p/. Effective pronunciation work makes the contrast perceptible (minimal pairs), adds a physical cue (word-initial English /p/ is voiceless and aspirated, so a paper strip moves), and then moves quickly into meaningful use. This is negative transfer of the L1 sound inventory and a normal part of acquisition.

traps.note: Constant public correction interrupts meaning-focused talk and raises the affective filter, and it gives no targeted perception or production practice.
Repeating a word list with no contrast and no context rarely transfers to spontaneous speech, and it never lets the student hear /p/ against /b/.
Substituting /b/ for /p/ is a predictable L1-transfer pattern for Arabic speakers. Persistence over a few months is typical and doesn't by itself suggest a speech disorder.

questions.key: Arabic lacks /p/: use minimal pairs (pea/bee) plus an aspiration cue, then meaningful practice, not drills or referral.

questions.stimulus: During a grade 8 social studies presentation, a student (Transitioning; home language Bengali) says, “Many families in the Sahara live in the de-ZERT.” Several classmates look puzzled, and one asks, “Like cake?”
questions.stem: The classmates' confusion is best explained by which feature of English pronunciation?
options: intonation, because the student used a rising pitch at the end of a statement
word stress, because stress placement can distinguish one English word from another
vowel epenthesis, because the student added an extra syllable to the word
allophonic variation, because the final /t/ in the word was not fully released by the speaker
questions.why: English has lexical (word) stress, and moving it can change the word: DEsert (dry land) vs. desSERT (sweet course), or noun–verb pairs like REcord/reCORD and PERmit/perMIT. Stress also changes vowel quality, because unstressed vowels often reduce to schwa /ə/. Listeners rely heavily on stress patterns to recognize words, so misplaced stress can block comprehension even when every individual sound is accurate.

traps.note: Intonation is the pitch pattern across a whole utterance; nothing in the scenario describes pitch. The problem is which syllable within one word was stressed.
No syllable was added; 'desert' and 'dessert' both have two. Only the stressed syllable moved.
How the final /t/ is released never changes which word an English listener hears. The confusion came from stress placement.

questions.key: English word stress can change the word: DEsert vs. desSERT, REcord (noun) vs. reCORD (verb).

questions.stimulus:
Grade 3 student (Emerging; home language Mandarin), same day
Oral retell: “Yesterday I walk to the par with my frien. We jump in the lea.”
Written retell: “Yesterday I walked to the park with my friend. We jumped in the leaves.”
questions.stem: Based on both samples, which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the student's oral omissions?
options: The student has not yet acquired the regular past tense, as the oral forms 'walk' and 'jump' show.
Mandarin syllables allow few final consonants, so the student drops word-final consonants and clusters in speech.
Mandarin verbs take no tense endings, so the student is transferring L1 grammar by leaving off -ed.
The omissions occur across many different words, which suggests a speech sound disorder needing evaluation.
questions.why: Mandarin syllables can end only in a vowel or a nasal (/n/ or /ŋ/), so English final stops, fricatives, and clusters are hard to pronounce. The key evidence is that the student drops final consonants in words with no grammatical ending (park, friend) and keeps a final /n/ (frien), while writing walked and jumped correctly. That points to phonological transfer of syllable structure, not a missing grammar rule.

traps.note: The oral sample alone suggests this, but the written retell shows walked and jumped used correctly. The omissions follow sound patterns, not grammar knowledge.
Mandarin does lack tense inflection, and that can cause grammatical omissions, but this student also drops non-grammatical finals (park, friend) and marks past tense correctly in writing.
The omissions are systematic and match Mandarin syllable structure, the hallmark of L1 transfer. They don't suggest a speech disorder.

questions.key: Compare oral and written evidence: dropped finals in speech but correct -ed in writing means phonological transfer, not missing grammar.

questions.stem: Using C for a consonant phoneme and V for a vowel phoneme, which word has the syllable structure CCCVCC?
options: splash
stamps
thrown
strict
questions.why: Syllable structure is described by phonemes, not letters. 'Strict' is /s t r ɪ k t/: three consonants before the vowel and two after. English allows up to three consonants at the start of a syllable (in that case the first is always /s/) and up to four at the end (texts), which is why learners whose languages favor simple CV or CVC syllables, such as Japanese or Mandarin, find English clusters difficult.

traps.note: 'Splash' begins with a three-consonant cluster, but sh is a single phoneme, /ʃ/, so the word is CCCVC.
'Stamps' has five consonants, but they fall two before the vowel and three after (/s t æ m p s/), so it is CCVCCC, the mirror image.
'Thrown' looks consonant-heavy, but th = /θ/ and ow = /oʊ/, so it is /θ r oʊ n/, only CCVC.

questions.key: Analyze syllables by phonemes: strict = /strɪkt/ = CCCVCC. Three-consonant onsets in English always begin with /s/.

questions.stimulus: A grade 10 student (Expanding; home language Spanish) reads aloud, “The banana is on the table.” The teacher notes that the student gives every syllable about the same length and a full vowel, saying [ba-na-na] with a clear [a] in each syllable.
questions.stem: The student's reading suggests a need for instruction in which feature of English pronunciation?
options: aspiration of voiceless stops at the beginning of stressed syllables
contrastive stress to highlight new information within a sentence
reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa in a stress-timed rhythm
rising intonation at the end of yes/no questions
questions.why: English is often described as stress-timed: stressed syllables are longer and louder, and many unstressed vowels reduce to schwa /ə/, so banana is /bəˈnænə/. Spanish is syllable-timed, with syllables of similar length and full vowels even when unstressed. Transferring that rhythm makes English sound choppy and can reduce intelligibility, so teaching stress and schwa (for example, tapping the stressed syllable) is high-yield.

traps.note: Aspiration is a real English feature some learners miss, but the teacher's notes describe equal syllable length and full vowels, which point to rhythm and vowel reduction.
Contrastive stress highlights one word in a sentence for meaning. The issue here is rhythm inside words: unstressed syllables aren't being reduced.
The sentence is a statement, so question intonation has nothing to do with this evidence.

questions.key: English is stress-timed: unstressed vowels reduce to schwa (/bəˈnænə/). Syllable-timed L1s like Spanish give every syllable full weight.

questions.stem: A teacher says to a student, “You turned in your permission slip, didn't you?” with falling intonation on the tag. What does the falling intonation most likely signal?
options: The teacher expects the student to confirm something the teacher already believes is true.
The teacher is genuinely unsure and is asking the student for new information.
No difference in meaning, since the words of the tag alone make the sentence a question.
The teacher is using contrastive stress to emphasize the word 'permission.'
questions.why: Intonation, the rise and fall of pitch across an utterance, carries meaning beyond the words. With a falling tag, the speaker is fairly sure and expects agreement; with a rising tag, the speaker is genuinely uncertain and wants information. ELLs may miss these cues or transfer L1 pitch patterns, so intonation is worth teaching explicitly in real exchanges.

traps.note: That meaning goes with rising intonation on the tag, which signals real uncertainty. A falling tag signals that the speaker expects confirmation.
The words are identical either way; the pitch pattern is what tells the listener whether the speaker is checking a belief or truly asking.
Contrastive stress makes one word prominent (the PERMISSION slip, not the lunch form). The stem describes pitch on the tag, which is intonation.

questions.key: Falling tag = the speaker expects confirmation; rising tag = a genuine question. Intonation carries meaning.

questions.stimulus:
Word | Student's pronunciation
bag | [bæk]
his | [hɪs]
card | [kɑrt]
love | [lʌf]
questions.stem: A grade 9 Expanding student whose home language is Russian reads a word list aloud. Voiced consonants at the beginning and in the middle of words are accurate (boy, ladder, visit), but the teacher records the pronunciations above. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Russian has no voiced consonants, so the student substitutes voiceless ones in every position.
The student is still in the silent period and is not yet ready for pronunciation instruction.
The student cannot hear voicing differences in any position, which suggests an auditory processing problem.
Russian makes voiced consonants voiceless at the end of a word, and the student is transferring that rule.
questions.why: Russian, like Polish and German, has final devoicing: voiced consonants such as /b d g z v/ become voiceless at the end of a word, so Russian хлеб ('bread') ends in [p]. Because this student voices consonants correctly at the beginning and middle of words, the issue is a positional L1 rule transferred to English. It can merge pairs like bag/back and his/hiss, so it's worth targeting with final-position minimal pairs.

traps.note: Russian has plenty of voiced consonants, and the student produces them correctly at the start and middle of words. Only word-final position is affected.
An Expanding ninth grader who reads aloud is far past the silent period, and pronunciation can be addressed at every level.
Correct voicing in initial and medial positions shows the student hears and makes the contrast. A position-specific pattern that matches the L1 is transfer, not a processing problem.

questions.key: Russian final devoicing makes 'bag' sound like 'back': a positional L1 rule, not a missing sound.

questions.stimulus:
Teacher says | Student writes
shop | chop
wash | wach
shoe | choo
questions.stem: A grade 2 Entering student whose home language is Spanish produces these spellings on a weekly spelling check. The pattern most likely reflects which of the following?
options: The student does not yet know the letter-sound correspondence for the letters s and h.
The student is confusing two allophones of a single English phoneme.
The student is reversing digraphs, which is an early warning sign of dyslexia.
Most varieties of Spanish have /tʃ/ but no /ʃ/, so the student hears English /ʃ/ as /tʃ/.
questions.why: /ʃ/ (shoe) and /tʃ/ (chew) are separate phonemes in English, as the minimal pair share/chair shows. Most varieties of Spanish have /tʃ/ (spelled ch, as in chico) but no /ʃ/ phoneme, so the new sound is mapped onto the closest familiar one, and the spelling follows what the student hears. This is transfer from the L1 phoneme inventory, best addressed with listening discrimination and minimal pairs.

traps.note: The student consistently writes ch, the spelling of the sound she hears. That points to a perception pattern, not a random gap in letter-sound knowledge.
In English, /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ are separate phonemes (share vs. chair). Treating them as allophones misreads the contrast.
A consistent substitution that matches the home language's sound system is typical L2 transfer. It is not a reversal and not a sign of dyslexia.

questions.key: Most Spanish varieties have /tʃ/ but no /ʃ/; sh-to-ch spellings reflect transfer from the L1 phoneme inventory.

questions.stimulus: The teacher's students walked home.
questions.stem: Which bound morpheme in this sentence is derivational?
options: the -s in students
the -ed in walked
the -'s in teacher's
the -er in teacher
questions.why: Derivational morphemes create a new word and often change its part of speech: -er turns the verb teach into the noun teacher. The other three are inflectional: plural -s, past tense -ed, and possessive -'s add grammatical information without creating a new word. English has only eight inflectional morphemes, and all of them are suffixes.

traps.note: Plural -s is one of the eight inflectional morphemes. 'Students' is still the same noun, just marked for number.
Past tense -ed is inflectional. 'Walked' is still a form of the verb walk, not a new word.
Possessive -'s is inflectional. It marks a grammatical relationship and doesn't create a new dictionary word.

questions.key: Derivational morphemes make new words (teach → teacher); inflectional ones (-s, -'s, -ed) only mark grammar.

questions.stem: Which of the following words contains exactly four morphemes?
options: caterpillars
mistreatments
uncomfortable
rewritten
questions.why: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning. 'Mistreatments' = mis- ('wrongly') + treat (free root) + -ment (derivational, verb → noun) + -s (inflectional plural): four morphemes in only three syllables. Counting morphemes means finding meaningful parts, not counting beats or letters.

traps.note: 'Caterpillars' has four syllables but only two morphemes: caterpillar (its pieces carry no meaning on their own) + plural -s.
'Uncomfortable' has five syllables but only three morphemes: un- + comfort + -able.
Close, but 'rewritten' has three morphemes: re- + write + -en (past participle). The doubled t is spelling, not a separate morpheme.

questions.key: Count morphemes by units of meaning: mis-treat-ment-s = 4, even though the word has only 3 syllables.

questions.stem: During a grade 5 Integrated ENL lesson, a student says, “Taller and teacher both end in -er, so they have the same kind of ending.” Which response best reflects accurate morphological analysis?
options: Yes. Both are derivational suffixes, because each one adds meaning to the base word.
No. Comparative -er in taller is inflectional; agentive -er in teacher is derivational.
Yes. Both are inflectional suffixes, because both of them are added to the end of a base word.
No. The -er in taller is a free morpheme, but the -er in teacher is a bound morpheme.
questions.why: The two endings sound the same but are different morphemes. Comparative -er is one of English's eight inflectional morphemes: tall and taller are both adjectives. Agentive -er is derivational: it creates a new word in a new class (teach, a verb → teacher, a noun). A quick test: if the part of speech changes or a new dictionary entry results, the morpheme is derivational.

traps.note: Both endings add meaning, so 'adds meaning' can't be the test. Comparative -er keeps tall an adjective, which makes it inflectional.
Many derivational morphemes are suffixes too (-ness, -ful, agentive -er). Position at the end of a word doesn't make a morpheme inflectional.
Neither -er can stand alone as a word, so both are bound. The real difference is inflectional vs. derivational.

questions.key: Same sound, different morphemes: comparative -er (taller) is inflectional; agentive -er (teacher) is derivational.

questions.stem: Which of the following words consists only of free morphemes?
options: bookcase
bookings
rebooked
booklets
questions.why: A free morpheme can stand alone as a word; a bound morpheme cannot. 'Bookcase' is a compound of two free morphemes, book + case. Each of the other words contains bound morphemes: -ing and -s, re- and -ed, and -let and -s.

traps.note: The -ing and -s in 'bookings' are bound suffixes that can't stand alone, even though book is free.
The prefix re- and the suffix -ed are bound morphemes; only book is free.
'Booklet' looks like book + let, but -let is a bound diminutive suffix (as in piglet), not the free word let.

questions.key: Free morphemes stand alone (book, case); a compound such as bookcase joins two free morphemes.

questions.stimulus:
Word wall, grade 6 Stand-alone ENL
brunch (breakfast + lunch)
motel (motor + hotel)
smog (smoke + fog)
Spanglish (Spanish + English)
questions.stem: All of the words on this word wall were formed by which word-formation process?
options: compounding
clipping
blending
back-formation
questions.why: Blending fuses parts of two words into one new word, usually the beginning of one and the end of the other: br(eakfast) + (l)unch. Compounding, by contrast, joins two whole words (notebook, classroom). Blends are a quick way to show students that English vocabulary keeps growing through predictable processes.

traps.note: Compounding combines whole words (classroom, notebook). These words fuse only parts of each source word.
Clipping shortens a single word (laboratory → lab). Each of these words merges two different source words.
Back-formation removes a supposed affix from one word (editor → edit). Nothing was removed from a single word here.

questions.key: Blend = parts of two words fused (brunch, smog); compound = two whole words joined (notebook).

questions.stimulus: A grade 11 student asks, “Did 'editor' come from 'edit,' the way 'teacher' came from 'teach'?” The teacher explains that 'editor' actually came first; 'edit' was created later when speakers removed what looked like the suffix -or.
questions.stem: The teacher is describing which word-formation process?
options: back-formation
clipping
derivation
conversion (zero derivation)
questions.why: Back-formation creates a new word by removing what speakers take to be an affix, usually producing a verb from a noun: editor → edit, babysitter → babysit, donation → donate. Clipping also shortens words, but it keeps the same meaning and part of speech (laboratory → lab). Back-formation produces a different word, typically in a new class.

traps.note: Clipping shortens a word without changing its meaning or class (examination → exam). 'Edit' is a new verb formed from the noun editor.
Ordinary derivation adds an affix (teach → teacher). Here an apparent affix was taken away, so the process runs in reverse.
Conversion changes a word's class with no change in form (a text → to text). 'Edit' is shorter than 'editor.'

questions.key: Back-formation removes a 'suffix' to coin a new word (editor → edit); clipping only shortens the same word (exam).

questions.stem: Which word is correctly paired with the process that formed it?
options: laser — blending
notebook — back-formation
babysit — acronym
exam — clipping
questions.why: 'Exam' is a clipping of 'examination': part of the word is cut off while the meaning and word class stay the same, as in lab, gym, and flu. Laser is an acronym (light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation), notebook is a compound of two free words, and babysit is a back-formation from babysitter.

traps.note: 'Laser' was built from the first letters of a phrase and is pronounced as a word, which makes it an acronym. A blend fuses parts of two words (smog).
'Notebook' joins two free words, note + book, so it's a compound. Nothing was removed.
'Babysit' was formed by removing -er from babysitter (back-formation). It isn't built from initial letters.

questions.key: Clipping cuts a word but keeps its meaning and class: examination → exam, laboratory → lab.

questions.stimulus:
Writing sample, grade 5 (Emerging; home language Mandarin)
“Yesterday my two brother play soccer in the park. My uncle car was very old, but it was fast.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the morphological pattern in this sample?
options: The student omits derivational suffixes, which points to limited depth of vocabulary knowledge.
The student omits inflectional endings for plural, past, and possession, a pattern consistent with the L1.
The student overgeneralizes regular inflections by adding them to irregular nouns and verbs.
The student shows a morphological processing weakness that warrants a special education referral.
questions.why: Plural -s, past -ed, and possessive -'s are all inflectional morphemes. Mandarin is an isolating language with little inflection: number, time, and possession are shown with numbers and measure words, time words and aspect particles, and the particle de (的). The student signals time with 'yesterday' and number with 'two,' so the meanings are there; the English inflectional endings are the instructional target.

traps.note: The missing endings (-s, -ed, -'s) are inflectional. They mark grammar, not new vocabulary.
Overgeneralization would look like 'childs' or 'goed.' Here endings are left out, not over-applied.
The omissions fit a predictable L1 pattern, and the student expresses the meanings with other words. That's typical acquisition, not evidence of a disability.

questions.key: Missing -s, -ed, and -'s are inflectional omissions, common when the L1 (e.g., Mandarin) marks these meanings without endings.

questions.stem: A grade 7 Integrated ENL science class includes several Transitioning ELLs whose home language is Spanish. The unit introduces 'photosynthesis,' 'photograph,' and 'synthesize.' Which approach best uses morphology to build the students' vocabulary?
options: Read each definition aloud while students copy it into vocabulary notebooks, then give a quiz at the end of the week.
Replace the technical terms in the reading with everyday phrases, such as 'how plants make food,' to reduce the load.
Have students break the words into parts (photo- 'light,' synth- 'put together') and link them to Spanish cognates.
Have students memorize a separate list of Greek and Latin roots before the unit, then begin the science content.
questions.why: Morphological analysis teaches students to break words into meaningful parts and use them to infer meaning, a strategy that transfers to new words such as photosensitive and synthetic. For Spanish speakers, many academic roots appear in cognates (fotosíntesis, fotografía, sintetizar), so linking the parts to the home language builds on an asset. The grade-level terms stay in place and are taught within the content.

traps.note: Copying definitions and taking a quiz is teacher-centered and gives students no strategy for working out related words.
Removing the academic terms waters down the content; ELLs need these words to read and write grade-level science.
Studying roots as an unconnected list before the unit separates morphology from meaning and context, so it rarely transfers.

questions.key: Teach morphological analysis in context (photo- + synthesis) and link word parts to home-language cognates.

questions.stem: Which statement about English morphology is accurate?
options: Every English suffix is inflectional.
Derivational morphemes never change a word's part of speech.
Inflectional morphemes create new words with their own dictionary entries.
Every English prefix is derivational.
questions.why: All eight English inflectional morphemes (plural -s, possessive -'s, third-person -s, past -ed, past participle -en/-ed, -ing, comparative -er, superlative -est) are suffixes, so every prefix (un-, re-, pre-, mis-, dis-) must be derivational. Suffixes can be either kind: -ness and -ful are derivational. Derivational morphemes often change word class, and they are what create new dictionary entries.

traps.note: Many suffixes are derivational (-ness, -ful, -tion, -ly). Only eight English suffixes are inflectional.
Derivational morphemes often change the class (teach → teacher, happy → happiness). Some don't (unhappy), but many do.
That describes derivation. Inflection only produces grammatical forms of the same word (walk, walks, walked).

questions.key: English has eight inflectional morphemes, all suffixes, so every English prefix is derivational.

questions.stimulus: A grade 8 student (Expanding; home language Bengali) reads aloud, “She jumped over the puddle and played outside,” pronouncing each -ed ending as an extra syllable: “jump-id,” “play-id.”
questions.stem: Which rule for pronouncing the past-tense ending should the teacher teach?
options: /ɪd/ after verbs ending in /t/ or /d/; /t/ after other voiceless sounds; /d/ after other voiced sounds
/ɪd/ after any consonant and /d/ after vowels, since -ed adds a syllable to most regular verbs
/ɪd/ after verbs ending in /t/ or /d/; /d/ after other voiceless sounds; /t/ after other voiced sounds
/ɪd/ for every regular verb, since the -ed spelling represents one fixed pronunciation
questions.why: The past-tense morpheme -ed has three allomorphs (predictable pronunciations), conditioned by the verb's final sound: /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (wanted, needed), /t/ after other voiceless sounds (jumped, washed), and /d/ after other voiced sounds, including vowels (played, cleaned). The ending matches the voicing of the sound before it. Plural -s follows the same logic: /ɪz/, /s/, /z/.

traps.note: It's right that -ed is /d/ after vowels (played), but /ɪd/ follows only /t/ and /d/. After other consonants -ed adds no syllable: jumped is one syllable.
This reverses the voicing match. A voiceless sound like /p/ takes voiceless /t/ (jumped); a voiced sound takes /d/.
This is exactly the student's error: reading the spelling. One spelling, -ed, represents three different pronunciations.

questions.key: -ed has three allomorphs: /ɪd/ after /t, d/; /t/ after voiceless sounds; /d/ after voiced (wanted, jumped, played).

questions.stimulus:
Journal entry, grade 6 (Transitioning; home language Korean)
“The math test was unpossible. My partner was unpolite to me, but later he said sorry.”
questions.stem: What do the words 'unpossible' and 'unpolite' best show about this student's morphological knowledge?
options: The student is attaching an inflectional morpheme to the wrong class of words.
The student has learned that un- means 'not' and is extending it to stems that take im-.
The student does not yet understand that adding a prefix changes a word's meaning.
The student is making random slips that suggest a weak memory for word forms.
questions.why: un-, in-/im-, dis-, and non- are all derivational prefixes meaning 'not,' and which one a stem takes is partly unpredictable (unhappy, impossible, impolite, dishonest). 'Unpossible' and 'unpolite' are rule-based forms: the student has abstracted un- as a productive prefix and is applying it beyond its range. This overgeneralization is evidence of growing morphological knowledge; the next step is teaching the in- family (impossible, illegal, irregular).

traps.note: un- is a derivational prefix, and English has no inflectional prefixes. The error is choosing the wrong derivational prefix.
The student used un- to mean 'not' exactly as intended, which shows clear understanding that prefixes change meaning.
Both forms follow the same rule (un- + adjective), so they are systematic developmental errors, not random slips.

questions.key: 'Unpossible' overgeneralizes productive un-, which shows rule learning. Teach which stems take im-, in-, il-, or ir-.

questions.stem: A teacher contrasts 'a GREENhouse' with 'a green HOUSE' (capitals show the stressed word). Which statement best explains the difference?
options: Both are compound nouns, and speakers shift the stress freely with no change in meaning.
'Greenhouse' is a blend of two words, while 'green house' is a compound noun.
'Greenhouse' contains a derivational morpheme, while 'green house' contains an inflectional one.
'Greenhouse' is a compound stressed on its first part; 'green house' is an adjective + noun phrase.
questions.why: Compounding joins two free morphemes into one word, and English noun compounds typically stress the first element: GREENhouse, BLACKboard, the WHITE House. A compound's meaning is often more than the sum of its parts (a greenhouse needn't be green). In the phrase 'a green HOUSE,' green is an adjective describing a house, and the main stress falls on the noun.

traps.note: The stress isn't free. It marks the difference between a compound (GREENhouse) and a phrase (green HOUSE), and the meanings differ.
A blend fuses parts of words (smog). 'Greenhouse' keeps both whole words, so it's a compound, and 'green house' is a phrase, not a compound.
Neither form contains an affix. Both are built from the free morphemes green and house.

questions.key: Compounds usually stress the first part and may have special meanings (GREENhouse); phrases stress the noun (green HOUSE).

questions.stem: Which word is built on a bound root rather than a free root?
options: replay
unkind
receive
helpful
questions.why: A root is the core of a word. A free root can stand alone (play, kind, help); a bound root cannot. In 'receive,' the root -ceive (from Latin capere, 'to take') never appears as a word on its own but recurs in conceive, deceive, and perceive. Many academic words are built on bound Latin and Greek roots (-struct-, -rupt-, -dict-), which is why root study supports content vocabulary.

traps.note: 'Play' stands alone as a word, so it's a free root; only the prefix re- is bound.
'Kind' is a free root; the prefix un- is the bound part.
'Help' is a free root; only the suffix -ful is bound.

questions.key: Bound roots can't stand alone (-ceive in receive, conceive); free roots can (play, help).

questions.stimulus:
Oral sample, grade 7 Integrated ENL social studies (Transitioning; home language Spanish)
“I am agree with Kevin. The colonists were angry because the taxes were not fair.”
questions.stem: The error in the student's first sentence is most likely the result of which of the following?
options: Negative transfer from Spanish, which expresses agreement with 'to be' plus a phrase (estoy de acuerdo).
A performance slip caused by speaking quickly, since the rest of the student's sample is grammatically accurate.
A gap in vocabulary knowledge, since the student is confusing the verb agree with the noun agreement.
Fossilization, since an error like this one shows that the student's interlanguage has stopped developing.
questions.why: In Spanish, agreement is expressed with estar plus a prepositional phrase: 'Estoy de acuerdo' ('I am in agreement'). The student maps that structure onto English, producing the copula am followed by agree as if it were an adjective. In English, agree is a verb that needs no be: 'I agree with Kevin.' Knowing the source tells the teacher exactly which contrast to teach.

traps.note: A slip is random and self-corrected. 'I am agree' is a well-known systematic pattern for Spanish speakers, so it's an error rooted in the L1.
The student uses agree with exactly the right meaning. The problem is the grammatical construction around the verb, not the vocabulary.
Fossilization means an error persists over a long period despite instruction. One sample can't show that; this is a transfer error that instruction can address.

questions.key: 'I am agree' transfers Spanish 'estoy de acuerdo' (be + phrase); in English, agree is a verb used without be.

questions.stimulus:
Writing sample, grade 9 (Emerging; home language Russian)
“Yesterday I bought new phone. Phone is very fast, and camera takes good pictures.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the pattern of errors in this sample?
options: Russian has no articles, so the student is still learning to mark English nouns as definite or indefinite.
The student is treating phone and camera as noncount nouns, which do not take articles in English.
The student is omitting subject pronouns, a pattern common among speakers of pro-drop languages.
The student is translating word for word from Russian, a habit best stopped by banning bilingual dictionaries.
questions.why: Russian, like Polish, Mandarin, Korean, and Japanese, has no articles, so English a/an and the represent a brand-new grammatical category: marking a noun as new to the listener (a new phone) or already identifiable (the phone). The errors are systematic omissions before singular count nouns, exactly where English requires an article. Teaching first mention (a) vs. second mention (the) in the student's own writing is a high-leverage next step.

traps.note: Phone and camera are being used as singular count nouns; countability isn't the issue. The missing articles are.
Every clause has a subject (I, Phone, camera). The missing words are articles, not pronouns.
Treating the home language as a habit to stamp out ignores how L1 knowledge can help target instruction. Bilingual resources support learning.

questions.key: Article omission is predictable when the L1 (Russian, Mandarin, Korean) has no articles; teach a (new) vs. the (known).

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: Amir was writing the lab report.
Amir has written the lab report.
The finished lab report is on Amir's desk.
The lab report was written by Amir.
questions.why: The passive voice is formed with a form of be plus a past participle (was written), and it makes the receiver of the action (the lab report) the subject. The agent can appear in a by-phrase or be left out entirely, which is common in science writing ('The solution was heated').

traps.note: 'Was writing' is be + -ing, the progressive aspect. Amir is still the doer and the subject, so the sentence is active.
'Has written' contains a past participle, but with have, not be. That's the present perfect in the active voice.
This sentence has a form of be, but no past participle and no action; is simply links the subject to a location.

questions.key: Passive = be + past participle (was written); the receiver becomes the subject, and the agent is optional.

questions.stimulus:
Personal narrative, grade 6 (Transitioning; home language Haitian Creole)
“Last summer my family go to Florida. We visit my aunt and we swim in the beach every day. My cousin show me her school. It was very big and have a library with computers.”
questions.stem: Which instructional focus would address the most significant pattern in this sample?
options: subject–verb agreement with third-person singular subjects, as in 'my cousin shows' and 'it has'
prepositions of place, as in swimming 'at the beach' rather than swimming 'in the beach'
past-tense verb forms, regular and irregular, taught within narrative writing
sentence combining, to turn the short, simple sentences into longer complex ones
questions.why: The dominant pattern is unmarked past tense: go, visit, swim, show, and have all need past forms in a narrative clearly set 'last summer,' and the student already uses was correctly. Haitian Creole marks time with preverbal particles (such as te for past) rather than verb endings, so English past inflection is a natural target. Teaching regular -ed and common irregular verbs in the student's own narrative addresses the most errors with the greatest effect on meaning.

traps.note: 'My cousin show' and 'have' look like agreement errors, but the story is set last summer, so the needed forms are showed and had: past tense, not shows and has.
'In the beach' is a real error, but it occurs once, while missing past tense appears in nearly every sentence.
Sentence combining is useful, but the sample already includes compound sentences, and the missing past tense affects meaning far more.

questions.key: Prioritize the most frequent, meaning-affecting pattern, and read errors in context: in a past narrative, 'show' needs 'showed,' not 'shows.'

questions.stem: In the sentence “Mariam has been studying English for three years,” the verb phrase is best described as which of the following?
options: past tense with perfect aspect, because the studying began in the past
present tense with perfect and progressive aspect
present tense with progressive aspect only, because of the -ing form
passive voice, because the main verb follows a form of be
questions.why: Tense locates an event in time and is marked on the first verb: has is present tense. Aspect shows how the event unfolds: have + past participle (been) marks perfect aspect, linking the past to now, and be + -ing (studying) marks progressive aspect, showing an ongoing activity. Together they form the present perfect progressive, used for an activity that began in the past and continues now, which is why 'for three years' fits.

traps.note: The studying began in the past, but tense is marked on has, which is present. The perfect aspect is what connects the past to now.
Progressive aspect is there (been studying), but has + been also marks perfect aspect, so 'progressive only' is incomplete.
Be + -ing is progressive. A passive needs be + past participle with the receiver as subject (English was studied by Mariam).

questions.key: Tense is marked on the first verb (has = present); aspect is perfect (have + participle) and/or progressive (be + -ing).

questions.stimulus: A grade 4 student (Expanding; home language Polish) stops the ENL teacher in the hallway and asks, “Do you know where is the nurse's office?”
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the student's error?
options: keeping question word order (verb before subject) inside an embedded question
omitting the auxiliary do, which English requires at the start of every question
attaching the possessive -'s to the wrong noun in the phrase 'the nurse's office'
using a yes/no question form in a situation that calls for a wh-question form
questions.why: In a direct wh-question, English inverts the subject and verb: 'Where is the nurse's office?' When that question is embedded inside another sentence ('Do you know…'), English returns to statement order: 'Do you know where the nurse's office is?' Learners from many language backgrounds keep the inversion well into the higher proficiency levels, so polite question frames are worth modeling explicitly.

traps.note: The main question already has do (Do you know…), and many questions need no do at all (Is it…?). The error is inverted word order inside the embedded clause.
'The nurse's office' is correct. The error is the position of is.
'Do you know where…?' is a correct and polite yes/no frame. The problem is the word order of the embedded part.

questions.key: Embedded questions use statement order: 'Do you know where the office is?' not 'where is the office?'

questions.stem: Which of the following is a complex sentence?
options: It rained all morning, but the game started on time.
Running to the bus, Maria dropped her science notebook.
Although it rained all morning, the game started on time.
Maria ran to the bus and dropped her science notebook in a puddle.
questions.why: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause. 'Although it rained all morning' has a subject and a verb but begins with a subordinating conjunction, so it can't stand alone. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction such as but, and a participial phrase like 'Running to the bus' has no subject–verb pair, so it isn't a clause at all.

traps.note: Two independent clauses joined by but make a compound sentence, not a complex one.
'Running to the bus' is a participial phrase with no subject or finite verb, so this is a simple sentence.
One subject (Maria) with two verbs is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.

questions.key: Complex = independent clause + dependent clause (Although…); compound = two independent clauses (…, but…).

questions.stimulus:
Writing sample, grade 3 (Entering; home language Urdu)
“I my homework finished. My brother cricket plays.”
questions.stem: The word order in these sentences most likely reflects which of the following?
options: The student is placing adverbs in the wrong position within each sentence.
The subject–object–verb word order of Urdu is transferring to English.
The student is attempting the passive voice but leaving out the auxiliary be.
The student has a language disorder that affects how sentences are formulated.
questions.why: English is a subject–verb–object (SVO) language, while Urdu, like Hindi, Bengali, Pashto, Korean, and Japanese, is subject–object–verb (SOV). The student places the object before the verb ('homework finished,' 'cricket plays') exactly as in the L1. This predictable negative transfer responds well to sentence frames and color-coded subject–verb–object sentence building.

traps.note: There are no adverbs in these sentences. The object (homework, cricket) comes before the verb.
A passive needs be + past participle with the receiver as subject. These are active sentences in SOV order.
Consistent SOV order from an Entering student is a textbook L1-transfer pattern, not a sign of a disorder.

questions.key: SOV home languages (Urdu, Bengali, Korean, Japanese) can produce 'I my homework finished'; English is SVO.

questions.stimulus:
Science journal, grade 8 (Expanding; home language Ukrainian)
“I did not know the word 'erosion,' so I looked up it in the glossary.”
questions.stem: Which explanation of the student's error is most accurate?
options: 'Look up' is an inseparable phrasal verb, so its object must be a noun rather than a pronoun.
'Look up' is a separable phrasal verb, and a pronoun object must go between the verb and particle.
'Up' is a preposition in this sentence, and the student chose the wrong preposition for the verb.
The student is transferring Ukrainian word order, which places object pronouns at the end of a clause.
questions.why: 'Look up' (search for information) is a separable phrasal verb: the verb and particle form one unit of meaning. With a noun object either order works ('looked up the word' or 'looked the word up'), but a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle: 'looked it up.' Inseparable phrasal verbs such as 'look after' and 'run into' never split ('look after her').

traps.note: 'Look up' (search) is separable: 'look the word up' is correct. Inseparable verbs like 'look after' keep the object after the particle, and any verb can take a pronoun object.
In 'look up' (search), up is a particle that belongs to the verb, and it is the right one. The problem is where the pronoun goes.
Nothing in the sample points to L1 word order, and the claim about Ukrainian is unsupported. Learners from many backgrounds make this error because the rule is specific to English phrasal verbs.

questions.key: Separable phrasal verbs put a pronoun object between verb and particle: 'look it up,' never 'look up it.'

questions.stimulus: Grade 8 Integrated ENL science. The lab text reads: “The water samples were collected by the students and then tested by the lab technician.” An Emerging ELL summarizes it as: “The water samples collected the students.”
questions.stem: Which instructional response would best address this misunderstanding?
options: Rewrite the lab text in the active voice so that ELLs at lower proficiency levels are not confused by passive sentences.
Assign a worksheet of twenty-five unrelated active sentences for the student to convert into the passive voice at home.
Explain that the passive voice is an advanced structure the student will study once she reaches the Expanding level.
Model how to find the doer in the text's passive sentences (be + participle, by-phrase), then have pairs label each one.
questions.why: Learners often rely on a 'first noun = doer' strategy, which works for active sentences but reverses the meaning of passives. Science texts use the passive constantly to keep the focus on the process rather than the agent, so ELLs need explicit help noticing be + past participle and the by-phrase, practiced on the actual grade-level text. This scaffolds the real text instead of simplifying it, and the pair work adds interaction and output.

traps.note: Removing the passives simplifies away the very language students must learn to read in science.
Converting unrelated sentences is decontextualized drill, and it practices production when the student's need is comprehension of the class text.
Passives are in the grade-level text now. Postponing instruction keeps the student from understanding current content.

questions.key: Learners read the first noun as the doer; teach passive cues (be + past participle, by-phrase) using the real content text.

questions.stimulus:
Argument essay, grade 10 (Expanding; home language Spanish)
“The education is very important for everyone. The science helps us understand the nature, and the music makes us happy.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the student's use of articles?
options: Spanish has no articles, so the student is guessing where English articles belong.
The student is confusing count and noncount nouns and adds the to every noncount noun.
The student is using the for emphasis, a stylistic feature of formal academic writing.
Spanish uses the definite article with abstract and generic nouns, where English uses none.
questions.why: Spanish requires the definite article with abstract nouns and with nouns used in a general sense: 'La educación es importante,' 'La música nos hace felices.' English uses the zero article in those cases ('Education is important,' 'Music makes us happy') and reserves the for specific, identifiable referents ('the music at the party'). This is transfer from an L1 that has articles with different rules, the opposite of the omission seen when the L1 has no articles.

traps.note: Spanish has definite and indefinite articles (el, la, un, una). The issue is a different rule for using them, not their absence.
These nouns are noncount, but noncount nouns can still take the when specific (the music at the party). The rule at issue is generic vs. specific reference.
English doesn't use the for emphasis in academic writing. The pattern matches Spanish article rules, not a style choice.

questions.key: Spanish uses the definite article for generic and abstract nouns ('la educación'); English uses none ('Education is…').

questions.stimulus:
Email to a teacher, grade 11 (Transitioning; home language French)
“Thank you for the advices. I found many informations for my project, and I finished all my homeworks.”
questions.stem: The student's errors involve which grammatical feature?
options: treating noncount nouns as count nouns, with plural -s and many
using irregular plural forms with nouns that have regular plurals
omitting the definite article before abstract or general nouns
overusing derivational suffixes to form new nouns from verbs
questions.why: Advice, information, and homework are noncount (mass) nouns in English: they take no plural -s and pair with much, a lot of, or some, or with a counter ('three pieces of advice'). Their French equivalents (des conseils, des informations, des devoirs) are count nouns that pluralize, so the student is transferring L1 countability. Countability is a grammatical property of how a language treats a noun, not a fact about the thing itself.

traps.note: The -s endings are regular plural forms. The issue is that these nouns don't take a plural at all in English.
The student does use the (the advices), and article use isn't the pattern. Plural -s on noncount nouns is.
Plural -s is inflectional, not derivational, and no new nouns are being formed.

questions.key: Countability is language-specific: advice, information, and homework are noncount in English but count in French and Spanish.

questions.stimulus:
Oral sample, grade 4 (Emerging; home language Arabic)
“My sister very smart. The library open now. My teacher from Egypt too.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the pattern in these sentences?
options: The student is leaving out the auxiliary do, which English requires in statements like these.
The student is producing telegraphic speech, which shows the student is in the preproduction stage.
Arabic does not use a present-tense form of 'be' in sentences like these, so the student omits is.
The student has an expressive language disorder, since small function words are missing from speech.
questions.why: In Arabic, present-tense equational sentences have no copula: the equivalent of 'My sister very smart' is fully grammatical. Each of the student's sentences lacks is exactly where English needs a linking verb before an adjective, adverb, or prepositional phrase. Russian and Haitian Creole also omit the present-tense copula in many sentences, so this transfer pattern is common in New York classrooms.

traps.note: English uses do in questions and negatives, not in affirmative statements like these. The missing word is is.
A student in preproduction produces little or no speech. These are complete thoughts missing one predictable word, which points to L1 transfer.
Only the copula is missing, systematically, and Arabic grammar predicts it. That's language transfer, not a disorder.

questions.key: Arabic (also Russian) has no present-tense copula, so 'My sister very smart' reflects L1 transfer.

questions.stimulus:
Oral sample, grade 10 (Expanding; home language Spanish)
“I live in the Bronx since 2022. Before that, I lived in Santo Domingo.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the error in the first sentence and its likely source?
options: 'Since' should be 'for,' because 2022 names a length of time rather than a starting point.
The verb should be simple past ('lived'), because the action began at a point in the past.
The verb should be present progressive ('am living'), because the situation is still going on.
English uses the present perfect ('have lived') for past-to-now states; Spanish uses present + desde.
questions.why: For a state that began in the past and continues into the present, English uses the present perfect ('I have lived in the Bronx since 2022') or the present perfect progressive ('have been living'). Spanish ('Vivo en el Bronx desde 2022'), like French and many other languages, uses the simple present here. The student's second sentence shows control of the simple past, so the gap is specifically the present perfect's past-to-now meaning.

traps.note: Since marks a starting point (since 2022); for marks a duration (for two years). The preposition is correct.
The simple past would mean the student no longer lives there. The situation continues now, which calls for the present perfect.
It's right that the situation is ongoing, but 'I am living here since 2022' is still ungrammatical; since + an ongoing situation needs the perfect.

questions.key: Past-to-now with since/for needs the present perfect ('have lived since 2022'); Spanish uses the simple present + desde.

questions.stem: Which pair of uses best illustrates polysemy rather than homonymy?
options: a baseball bat / a bat flying at night
the mouth of a river / a person's mouth
flour for baking / a flower in the garden
a lead pipe / to lead the class
questions.why: Polysemy is one word with several related meanings that grew from a shared core, often by metaphor: a river's mouth is where it opens, like a person's mouth. Homonyms are unrelated words that happen to share a form; bat the animal and bat the club have different origins. Content classes are full of polysemous words (a table in math, a cell in science), and students can use the core meaning to infer the new sense.

traps.note: The two bats are unrelated words that share a spelling and sound. That's homonymy, not one word with related senses.
Flour and flower are different words that only sound alike (homophones), with different spellings and meanings.
The two leads are spelled alike but pronounced differently (/lɛd/, /lid/) and are unrelated words: homographs.

questions.key: Polysemy = one word with related senses (the mouth of a river); homonymy = unrelated words sharing a form (bat).

questions.stimulus: During a grade 3 lesson, the teacher says to a newcomer (Entering; home language Wolof), “Can you close the door?” The student smiles, says “Yes,” and stays seated.
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the student's response?
options: The student responded to the literal form, a question about ability, rather than to its function as a request.
The student does not yet know the verb close and answered 'Yes' simply to avoid seeming confused.
The student was being deliberately uncooperative and needs a clearer behavioral expectation from the classroom teacher.
The student is in the silent period and so could not yet produce a full verbal response to the teacher.
questions.why: A speech act is what an utterance does: request, apologize, invite, refuse. 'Can you close the door?' is a question in form but a request in function, an indirect speech act. A newcomer may process the literal meaning (Are you able to?) and answer it accurately. Interpreting indirect speech acts is part of pragmatic competence and develops with explicit modeling ('When a teacher asks Can you…?, it means Please do it').

traps.note: Nothing shows a vocabulary gap; 'Yes' is an accurate answer to the literal question. The gap is in interpreting the utterance's function.
Reading a pragmatic misunderstanding as defiance blames the student for a normal stage in learning English conventions.
A student in the silent period typically doesn't speak, but this student answered. The issue is pragmatic interpretation, not readiness to produce speech.

questions.key: 'Can you close the door?' is an indirect speech act: question form, request function. Newcomers may answer the literal form.

questions.stimulus:
A grade 10 Expanding student reads this exchange in a novel:
Daniela: “So, is the new coach any good?”
Marcus: “Well, he's always on time.”
The student writes: “Marcus thinks the coach is good because he is on time.”
questions.stem: The student's interpretation shows difficulty with which aspect of meaning?
options: connotation, because the phrase 'on time' carries a negative emotional association in English
implicature, because Marcus's limited answer implies a negative opinion of the coach
idiom, because the phrase 'on time' cannot be understood from the meanings of its words
polysemy, because the word 'good' has several related meanings in English
questions.why: Implicature is meaning a speaker implies beyond the literal words. Grice's Cooperative Principle predicts that listeners assume a reply is relevant and as informative as needed, so when Marcus answers a question about quality with only a minor positive detail, readers infer he has nothing better to say. Literary dialogue relies heavily on implicature, and 'What does the character say? What does the character mean?' charts help ELLs read between the lines.

traps.note: 'On time' has a positive or neutral association. The hidden meaning comes from what Marcus chooses not to say.
'On time' is transparent, and the student understood it correctly. The missed meaning is implied, not idiomatic.
The student understood 'good' correctly. The misreading is about what Marcus's reply implies, not about a word's multiple senses.

questions.key: Implicature is meaning implied beyond the words (faint praise = criticism). Teach 'says vs. means' with dialogue.

questions.stimulus:
Personal essay, grade 7 (Transitioning; home language Nepali)
“My grandfather is very stubborn. He never gave up learning English, even at 65 years old, and our whole family admires him.”
questions.stem: Which aspect of word meaning should the teacher address in feedback on this sample?
options: denotation, because 'stubborn' does not refer to a person who refuses to change course
register, because 'stubborn' is too informal a word to use in a written essay
connotation, because 'stubborn' has a negative association that clashes with the admiring tone
collocation, because the intensifier 'very' cannot be used to modify 'stubborn'
questions.why: Denotation is a word's literal meaning; connotation is the emotional or evaluative association it carries. 'Stubborn' and 'determined' share a similar denotation (unwilling to give up), but stubborn sounds critical, which clashes with 'our whole family admires him.' Shades-of-meaning work, such as placing synonyms on a negative-to-positive scale, helps ELLs choose words that match their intent.

traps.note: The literal meaning fits: the grandfather refused to give up. The problem is the negative feeling the word carries.
'Stubborn' is a standard, neutral-register word that appears in formal writing. Its issue is evaluative tone, not formality.
'Very stubborn' is a natural English collocation. The problem is the word's negative association.

questions.key: Denotation = literal meaning; connotation = emotional association (stubborn vs. determined). Teach shades of meaning.

questions.stimulus: During a partner task, a grade 5 Emerging student needs a stapler but doesn't know the word. She says, “Can I borrow the… the thing you push to put papers together?”
questions.stem: The student is demonstrating which component of communicative competence, as defined by Canale and Swain?
options: grammatical competence
sociolinguistic competence
discourse competence
strategic competence
questions.why: Strategic competence is the ability to keep communication going when knowledge runs out, using strategies such as circumlocution (describing the word), gesture, approximation, or asking for help. Canale and Swain's model has four components: grammatical (rules of words, sentences, and sounds), sociolinguistic (appropriateness to context), discourse (connecting sentences into cohesive, coherent text), and strategic. This student's circumlocution is a strength worth naming.

traps.note: Grammatical competence is knowledge of vocabulary, morphology, syntax, and pronunciation. The student is compensating for a missing word, not displaying grammatical knowledge.
Sociolinguistic competence is adjusting language to the setting and listener (politeness, register). The key move here is talking around a vocabulary gap.
Discourse competence is connecting ideas across sentences. This is a single repair strategy within one utterance.

questions.key: Strategic competence = repairing breakdowns (circumlocution, gesture, asking). Canale & Swain: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, strategic.

questions.stimulus:
A grade 11 student (Expanding; home language Pashto) sends this email to the assistant principal:
“hey!! wats up? i need u to sign my form 4 the trip asap. thx”
questions.stem: Which response by the ENL teacher would best develop the student's sociolinguistic competence?
options: Have the student compare the email with a version for an administrator, noting greeting, word choice, and tone, then revise.
Return the email with every spelling and capitalization error circled so that the student can correct each one before sending it again.
Tell the student that texting language is incorrect English and that it should be avoided in every setting, including with friends.
Give the student a list of formal vocabulary words to memorize and use in all school writing, starting with the next email.
questions.why: Sociolinguistic competence, one of Canale and Swain's four components, is the ability to match language to audience, setting, and purpose. The student's texting register (hey!!, u, asap) works with friends but not with an administrator. Contrasting the same message for two audiences lets the student notice register features and revise, treating informal English as a resource with its own place rather than as an error.

traps.note: Marking every surface error treats the email as a spelling problem and misses the real issue, register. It also tends to raise anxiety without teaching audience awareness.
Informal registers are legitimate and useful; labeling them 'incorrect' devalues the student's language. The goal is choosing the right register for the setting.
A memorized word list doesn't teach how greetings, requests, and tone shift with audience, and 'use in all school writing' ignores context.

questions.key: Teach register by contrasting the same message for different audiences; informal English is a resource with its own place.

questions.stimulus: During a grade 5 read-aloud, the class reads: “Right before the spelling bee, Ana got cold feet and almost went home.” A Transitioning student whose home language is Haitian Creole asks, “Why were her feet cold? Was it winter?”
questions.stem: Which teacher response would best support the student's comprehension?
options: Give the meaning in a few words and keep reading, so that the class does not lose the thread of the story at an exciting moment.
Name 'got cold feet' as an idiom meaning 'got too nervous,' point to story clues, and invite similar home-language expressions.
Skip idioms during read-alouds, since figurative language is beyond what students at the Transitioning level can understand.
Have the student look up 'cold' and 'feet' in a picture dictionary so that the student can work out the meaning independently.
questions.why: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning can't be worked out from its individual words; the student's question shows a literal reading of 'cold feet.' Naming the expression as an idiom, giving its meaning, and tying it to context clues ('almost went home') teaches a strategy, not just a definition. Inviting home-language equivalents treats students' languages as a resource and deepens the class's understanding of figurative language.

traps.note: A quick gloss fixes this one phrase but gives no strategy for recognizing idioms and no chance for students to engage with the language.
Figurative language is part of grade-level texts, and Transitioning students can learn idioms with support. Skipping them lowers expectations.
Idioms are non-compositional, so looking up each word produces the literal reading that confused the student in the first place.

questions.key: Idioms are non-compositional: name them, explain them in context, and connect them to home-language expressions.

questions.stimulus: In a grade 9 Integrated ENL English class, the teacher notices that during whole-class discussions, a Transitioning student (home language Tibetan) begins to speak only after a long pause, by which time classmates have already jumped in. She rarely gets a turn, though her written responses show strong ideas.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most effective response?
options: Explain to the student that American classrooms reward speaking up quickly, and encourage her to interrupt as her classmates do.
Reduce the weight of discussion in her participation grade, since her written work already shows strong understanding of the text.
Use structured turn-taking, such as think-pair-share, talking chips, or set wait time, so every student has a protected turn.
Refer the student to the school counselor, since her hesitation in discussions suggests she may have significant social anxiety.
questions.why: Turn-taking norms, such as how long a pause signals that someone else may speak and whether overlapping talk is friendly or rude, vary across speech communities and individuals. Fast, overlapping discussion favors students whose norms match it. Structured protocols and deliberate wait time give every student a turn and processing time, increasing ELL output without asking anyone to abandon their own norms.

traps.note: Telling her to imitate classmates treats her conversational norms as the problem. Changing the discussion structure equalizes access instead.
Lowering oral expectations removes practice she needs. The goal is access to discussion, not exemption from it.
A longer pause before speaking, together with strong written work, fits different turn-taking norms and processing time, not a clinical concern.

questions.key: Turn-taking norms vary; use structured talk protocols and wait time so every ELL gets a protected turn.

questions.stimulus:
Writing sample, grade 4 (Transitioning; home language Uzbek)
“My family came to New York in 2023. My family lived with my uncle first. My uncle has a small apartment. The small apartment is in Brooklyn. My family moved to a new apartment in June.”
questions.stem: Which instructional focus would most improve the flow of this paragraph?
options: verb tense consistency, so that every sentence in the paragraph uses the simple past tense
cohesive devices, such as pronoun reference (we, it, there), to link sentences without repeating nouns
more precise and vivid vocabulary, such as replacing 'small' with a word like 'cramped' or 'tiny'
capitalization of proper nouns, such as the place names New York and Brooklyn in the paragraph
questions.why: Cohesion is created by explicit links between sentences: reference (pronouns such as we, it, there), conjunctions and transitions (first, then), substitution, ellipsis, and lexical ties. The student repeats full noun phrases (my family, the small apartment) where English would usually switch to pronouns, so the paragraph is accurate but choppy. Teaching reference ties and simple sequence transitions builds discourse competence.

traps.note: The tense shifts are logical: has and is describe what is still true. Tense isn't what makes the paragraph choppy.
Richer vocabulary can help, but it doesn't fix the repeated nouns that break the flow between sentences.
New York and Brooklyn are already capitalized, so this focus doesn't match the evidence.

questions.key: Cohesion comes from explicit ties: pronoun reference, transitions, substitution, lexical links. Repeated nouns signal a need for reference.

questions.stimulus:
Science paragraph, grade 8 (Expanding; home language Bengali)
“Plants need sunlight. Furthermore, my cousin has a garden. Therefore, the sun is a star. In addition, some stars are very far away. As a result, we watered the plants.”
questions.stem: Which statement best describes this paragraph?
options: It lacks cohesion, because it contains no words that connect one sentence to the next.
It is coherent, because transition words link each sentence to the one before it.
It uses many cohesive devices but lacks coherence, because its ideas are not logically related.
It is coherent but lacks cohesion, because its ideas are logical but poorly linked together.
questions.why: Cohesion is the surface linking of sentences through explicit devices such as transitions, pronouns, and repetition. Coherence is the underlying logical sense of the whole that a reader can follow. This paragraph is full of transitions (Furthermore, Therefore, As a result), but they signal relationships that don't exist between the ideas, so it is cohesive on the surface yet incoherent. ELLs sometimes add transitions from a list without matching their meaning, so teach what each one signals.

traps.note: The paragraph is packed with transition words (Furthermore, Therefore, In addition). Their absence isn't the problem.
Transitions create surface cohesion, but they can't make unrelated ideas logical. Coherence depends on meaningful connections.
This reverses the terms. The ideas are what's illogical; the linking words are plentiful.

questions.key: Cohesion = surface ties (transitions, pronouns); coherence = logical sense. A text can be cohesive yet incoherent.

questions.stimulus: A grade 6 student (Emerging; home language Spanish) writes: “It was raining very hard. However, the soccer game was canceled.”
questions.stem: What is the most accurate description of the problem in the second sentence?
options: The discourse marker signals contrast, but the ideas have a cause-and-effect relationship.
The second sentence is a fragment, because it begins with a transition word and a comma.
The verb 'was canceled' should be changed to the active voice to make the sentence clearer to readers.
The marker 'however' is too informal a choice for written academic English.
questions.why: Discourse markers (transitions) signal how ideas relate: however and on the other hand signal contrast; therefore, as a result, and so signal cause and effect; in addition signals addition. Heavy rain causing a cancellation is cause and effect, so the sentence needs 'As a result' or 'Therefore.' Teaching markers grouped by function, with examples, prevents this kind of mismatch.

traps.note: 'However, the soccer game was canceled' has a subject and a finite verb, so it's a complete sentence. The marker's meaning is the problem.
The passive is natural here, since who canceled the game doesn't matter. Voice doesn't affect the logic between the sentences.
'However' is standard, even formal, written English. It simply signals the wrong relationship.

questions.key: Match discourse markers to the relationship: contrast (however), cause–effect (therefore, as a result), addition (in addition).

questions.stimulus: A grade 8 Transitioning student (home language Dari) walks up to a substitute teacher's desk and says, in a calm and friendly tone, “Give me the paper for homework.” The substitute later reports that the student was “rude.”
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this interaction?
options: The student made a grammatical error, since English imperatives require a stated subject such as 'you.'
The student's culture places little value on politeness toward teachers, which the school should address.
The student is still learning English ways to soften requests (Could I please…?), so the imperative sounded abrupt.
The student probably used a rising intonation, which made the request sound like a challenge to the substitute teacher.
questions.why: English usually softens requests to teachers and other adults with modals and indirect forms ('Could I have…?', 'May I please…?'). A bare imperative is grammatically correct, but the student is still acquiring these pragmatic conventions, so the request sounds more direct than intended. Misreading such gaps as rudeness is common; teaching request forms explicitly through role plays with different listeners builds pragmatic competence.

traps.note: English imperatives normally omit 'you' (Give me…, Open your books), so the sentence is grammatical. The issue is social appropriateness.
Nothing supports a claim about the student's culture, and the friendly tone shows no intent to be disrespectful. The gap is in English request conventions.
The scenario describes the tone as calm and friendly and says nothing about intonation. The bare imperative explains the reaction.

questions.key: Pragmatic gaps such as unsoftened requests aren't rudeness; explicitly teach polite request forms like 'Could I please…?'

questions.stimulus: A grade 3 teacher builds a concept map for a science unit: TREE at the top, with branches leading to OAK, MAPLE, and PINE.
questions.stem: The relationship between 'oak' and 'tree' is an example of which semantic relation?
options: synonymy
antonymy
meronymy
hyponymy
questions.why: A hyponym is a more specific word included in a broader category word, its hypernym: oak, maple, and pine are hyponyms of tree. Meronymy, by contrast, is a part–whole relation (branch, root, and leaf are parts of a tree). Organizing vocabulary by semantic relations in concept maps helps ELLs learn words in connected networks instead of isolated lists.

traps.note: Synonyms have nearly the same meaning (big/large). An oak is a kind of tree, not another word for tree.
Antonyms are opposites (hot/cold). Oak and tree aren't opposites.
Meronymy is part to whole (branch → tree). An oak isn't part of a tree; it's a type of tree.

questions.key: Hyponymy = 'kind of' (oak → tree); meronymy = 'part of' (branch → tree).

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Dell Hymes's contribution to the concept of communicative competence?
options: He divided communicative competence into four components: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, and strategic.
He proposed that comprehensible input slightly beyond the learner's current level is what drives acquisition.
He argued that an innate language acquisition device explains how every child acquires grammar.
He argued that knowing a language includes knowing when, where, and to whom to say what, not only grammar.
questions.why: Dell Hymes coined 'communicative competence' as a response to Chomsky's narrower notion of linguistic competence (knowledge of grammar). Hymes argued that speakers also know how to use language appropriately in social context: when to speak, what to say, to whom, and how. Canale and Swain later defined its components, and the concept underlies Communicative Language Teaching.

traps.note: Right idea, wrong theorists: the four-part breakdown comes from Canale and Swain, who built on Hymes's concept.
This is Krashen's Input Hypothesis (i+1), a theory of how acquisition happens, not a definition of communicative competence.
The innate LAD is Chomsky's idea. Hymes's point was that Chomsky's grammar-only view of competence leaves out social use.

questions.key: Hymes coined communicative competence (appropriate use, not just grammar); Canale & Swain named its four components.
